newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Upbeat investors brave power cuts in Russia Far East.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Upbeat investors brave power cuts in Russia Far East.

text.p: Andrew Fox is so robustly upbeat about business prospects in the far-flung corner of Russia that he has chosen to make his home.

"Taking a long-term view you have to be optimistic about this region. Of course there are problems but investment is increasing. Vladivostok is becoming part of the Pacific Rim economy," said Fox, a youthful British-born stockbroker.

His Tiger Securities provides a good illustration of how Vladivostok's position on Russia's Far Eastern seaboard, seven time zones and 7,000 km (4,500 miles) away from Moscow, can be turned to commercial advantage.

Under a deal sealed earlier this year with Regent European Securities, part of the Hong Kong-based Regent Pacific Group, Fox's company now sells Russian blue chip stocks to Asian and other Pacific Rim investors in their own time zone.
"Vladivostok could some day become Russia's second big financial centre," said Fox.
RESOURCE-RICH REGION BATTERED BY POWER CUTS, WAGE DELAYS

It is not difficult to see the Russian Far East's attractions for foreign investors. Only an hour's flight from Japan, it is rich in oil, gas, timber, gold, diamonds, metals and fish and has an extensive transport network.
It is home to Russia's three largest sea shipping firms and four of the country's nine biggest ports, accounting for 40 percent of national dry cargo turnover.
But a casual visitor roaming the pothole-ridden streets of this city of 700,000, which only opened to outsiders five years ago, might be forgiven for taking a more sceptical view.

A short distance from Fox's office, hundreds of protesters gather outside the imposing local government building to demand the resignation of regional governor Yevgeny Nazdratenko and to express their rage over chronic power cuts and wage arrears.

Like millions of people across the Russian Federation local miners and many other workers go months without pay due to a vicious circle of debt linking producers and customers, government and private sector.

Adding insult to injury, the citizens of Primorsky Krai region -- of which Vladivostok is the capital -- also endure frequent electricity blackouts because of heavy debts accumulated in the energy sector.
Some areas of Primorsky Krai are often without electricity and hot water for more than 20 hours a day.
REGION'S FUTURE HINGES ON EXPORTS, OUTSIDE CONTACTS
"The energy crisis has a very adverse effect on business development here," said Viktor Tumanov, chief representative of ING Bank, the only Western bank with a branch in Vladivostok.

But he said many businesses, including the main hotels and restaurants, had solved the problem by installing their own generators. Central Vladivostok seems largely unmarked by the power cuts that have become such a way of life in the suburbs.
Tumanov echoed Fox's optimism about Vladivostok's prospects.
"There are businesses here succeeding, finding markets for their products, especially in the food industry, in timber, mining and transport," he said.
"Slowly the region is developing contacts abroad but it takes time. We are used to Moscow taking all the decisions."
Recent statistics showed that hard currency investments in Vladivostok were up 18 percent in 1996 from the previous year, with the biggest growth in transport and communications.
SOUTH KOREANS, JAPANESE, U.S. LOOK TO LONG TERM

Perhaps the most visible sign of outside confidence in Vladivostok's future is a vast new steel structure erected by South Korea's Hyundai Corp in the centre of town that will house a business centre. The investment is worth some $100 million.
Hyundai, looking to the long haul like many other South Korean investors here, is also considering developing a seaside resort area near Vladivostok.

Japan's big trading houses like Mitsubishi, Mitsui and Sumitomo are all represented in Vladivostok and are keen to tap the region's abundant natural resources but they take a generally more cautious investment stance than the South Koreans, due partly to a long-running territorial dispute.
Tokyo claims four tiny islands seized by Moscow at the end of World War Two. Despite Russia's refusal to return the islands, relations with Japan have recently been improving.
Japanese firms are particularly interested in the development of oil and gas reserves off Sakhalin Island to the northeast of Vladivostok, worth billions of dollars.
These projects will have a long-term, cumulative impact on Vladivostok's own economy, businessmen said.

The Russian Far East has been identified by the United States as a priority region for American investment, which currently totals about $200 million annually, mainly in the food import and telecommunications sectors.
BUSINESS KEEPS WARY EYE ON LOCAL POLITICAL BATTLES

Both foreign and Russian investors still face formidable obstacles. As elsewhere in Russia, they cite cumbersome bureaucracy, high and contradictory taxes arbitrarily enforced and -- especially damaging for a region so far from European markets -- crippling railway tariffs.
Vladivostok is hampered by a heavy preponderence of Soviet-era military plants, reflecting its status as home to the once mighty but now cash-strapped Pacific Fleet.
Politics, in the guise of a long-running dispute between the regional and city authorities, has also given investors cause for concern and stymied efforts to resolve the power shortages.
Mayor Viktor Cherepkov has accused Governor Nazdratenko of helping engineer the energy crisis by opposing higher electricity tariffs. The governor says these will hurt industry.

The crisis has taken its toll on the popularity of Nazdratenko, who had been close to some of President Boris Yeltsin's former conservative advisers but is known to be on bad terms with reformers like Finance Minister Anatoly Chubais who now wield the power in the Kremlin.
The governor's spokeswoman Nataliya Vstovskaya said it was unfair to blame Nazdratenko for all Primorsky Krai's ills in a system where power remains concentrated in distant Moscow.
"You can't separate our problems here from the broader crisis in Russia's economy," she told Reuters.
"We don't want confrontation with the centre, we just want them to listen to us more," she added.
